Commission in its analysis of Dauphin Island’s certificate application in the above-referenced docket.
Dauphin Island’s responses are attached.

This filing contains Privileged information consisting of revised sensitive environmental resource
information. These files have been removed from the public document and marked as CUI//PRIV. Dauphin
Island requests that the enclosed Privileged information be accorded privileged treatment and placed in a
non-public file.

Consistent with Section 385.2005(a) of the Commission’s regulations, the undersigned has read this filing
and knows its contents; the contents are true as stated, to the best of his knowledge and belief; and the
undersigned possesses full power and authority to sign this filing.

Consistent with Section 385.2010 of the Commission’s regulations, Dauphin Island is serving copies of this
filing to each person whose name appears on the official service list for this proceeding.

2. Indicate who would own the onshore site/right-of-way after completion of abandonment
activities. If abandoned aboveground facilities would not be removed, explain why and describe
how DIGP would continue to maintain these facilities.
Response:
Following completion of the proposed abandonment activities, the DIGP-owned and operated
facilities included within the Section 7(b) abandonment application will be abandoned in place or
removed as described in RR1 of the original application. The abandonment scope is limited to
DIGP facilities through the applicable custody transfer/interconnection points.
The DIGP aboveground facilities located on the plant property that are included within the
abandonment scope will be transferred to Esfeller Properties, LLC on an “as-is, where-is” basis.
Prior to transfer, these facilities and associated pipelines will be placed in a gas-free, non-
operational, and non-hazardous condition. Following transfer, Esfeller Properties, LLC will
assume responsibility for the transferred aboveground facilities, including their continued
maintenance. DIGP will not operate or maintain these facilities following the transfer.
DIGP pipelines approved for abandonment in place and the associated rights-of-way will remain
in place following completion of the abandonment activities. Esfeller has agreed to allow the DIGP
pipelines to remain abandoned in place and to provide DIGP permanent access to the abandoned
pipelines.

3. Characterize the environmental baseline of the project area by identifying physiographic
characteristics (e.g. climate, topography, etc), how the environment has changed over time, general
environmental trends, and any environmental concerns in the project area.
Response:
The Project area extends from coastal portions of southern Mobile County, Alabama, through
Portersville Bay and Mississippi Sound into state and federal offshore waters in the Mobile and
Main Pass blocks of the Gulf of America. This setting encompasses low-lying coastal land, shallow
estuarine waters, and the open continental shelf. The Project is located within the East Gulf
Coastal Plain Section of the Coastal Plain physiographic province (U.S. Geological Survey
[USGS], 2023). Terrain is generally level to gently sloping, with onshore elevations ranging from
approximately 0 to 17 feet above sea level and offshore depths reaching approximately 257 feet
below sea level (Google Earth, 2026). Onshore geologic materials include alluvial, coastal, and
low terrace deposits containing quartz sand and shell fragments with clay lenses; offshore deposits
include marine deposits of quartz sand, silt, clay, peat, and ooze (USGS, 2017a).
The onshore environment contains wetlands, upland forests, and developed land. Wetlands
identified during Project surveys include palustrine emergent, scrub-shrub, and forested wetlands.
Developed areas include paved, graveled, and routinely maintained portions of existing industrial
facilities and associated infrastructure. Onshore recreational activities include the nearby
Portersville Bay Wetlands Tract, a 470-acre nature preserve consistent of coastal marsh, piney
flatwoods, and maritime forest with recreational activities such as wildlife and bird watching
(Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources [ADCNR], 2026a; Alabama
Forever Wild, 2020). The adjoining coastal waters support fish and shellfish habitats as well as
commercial and recreational uses. Additionally, there are artificial reefs located in the offshore
Project vicinity, which provide foraging, spawning, and shelter habitats for fish, as well as
recreational saltwater fishing and scuba diving opportunities (ADCNR, 2026b).
Climate in the Mobile area is characterized by warm, humid summers and comparatively mild
winters. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Climate at a Glance tool
using the 1996-2026 climate normal period indicate normal average daily minimum temperatures
of approximately 40°F in January and normal average daily maximum temperatures of
approximately 91°F in July (NOAA, 2026a). These observations characterize the regional
mainland climate; coastal offshore conditions can vary. Tropical storms and hurricanes are
important environmental disturbances in the Project area, capable of rapidly changing shorelines,
redistributing sediment, and inundating low-lying coastal areas. USGS investigations document
long-term beach erosion, breaching at the island’s narrowest extent, and infrastructure damage
at Dauphin Island associated with Hurricanes Ivan and Katrina (USGS, 2017b).
                            Dauphin Island Gathering Partners
                Dauphin Island Gathering Partners Abandonment Project
                                Docket No. CP26-560-000
            Response to October 16th, 2026 Environmental Information Request

Mississippi Sound is a shallow, brackish estuary situated between mainland Alabama and offshore
barrier islands, including Dauphin Island. Barrier islands along the southern edge of the sound
separate the microtidal estuary from the Gulf of America. The estuary developed through
changing sea levels, river deposition, and tidal processes over thousands of years (USGS, 2025).
Sediment movement is a natural process of this setting; barrier island protection from Gulf wave
action mediates current flow within the sound, resulting in predominantly fine-grained sediment
deposition along the seafloor (USGS, 2025). Offshore turbidity in the Project area therefore
varies with physical conditions and sediment availability, rather than representing a fixed
characteristic throughout the marine Project area.
Human activities have also modified the regional coastal environment. In the neighboring Mobile
Bay, which exchanges water with Mississippi Sound through Pass aux Herons, man-made
channels, drainage areas, and oyster reefs have significantly altered circulation (NOAA, 2026b).
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) 1992 analysis of trends in Gulf coastal
habitats document marsh conversion associated with direct and indirect effects of dredged-
material disposal in the Mobile Bay region. It also reported that a study in Mobile Bay revealed
emergent marsh habitat declined by more than 10,000 acres, or 35 percent, between 1955 and
1979, with half of this loss resulting from industrial, commercial, and residential development;
other losses were the result of erosion and/or subsidence (EPA, 1992). In addition, at the time of
the report, the hydrology of the Mobile Bay had been markedly altered through excavation of a
deep channel through the center of the Bay and the profusion of spoil areas in open water (EPA,
1992). These historical findings demonstrate that the present coastal landscape reflects both
human modification and natural shoreline processes; however, they do not establish a current
annual loss rate.
More recent shoreline investigations document continued coastal change. A USGS assessment
examining approximately 75 years of shoreline positions found erosion along both Gulf-facing
and back-barrier shorelines of Dauphin Island and Little Dauphin Island, resulting in decreasing
island widths. Storm overwash and breaching can also move sediment toward back-barrier
environments, producing localized deposition. Coastal change therefore involves erosion,
sediment redistribution, and island migration rather than uniform shoreline retreat. The
assessment identified cross-barrier sediment exchange as an important process sustaining island
width, as well as identified human activities such as development, post-storm recovery, and
restoration as affecting the long-term sustainability of barrier island systems (USGS, 2018). These
changes matter to surrounding habitats because Dauphin Island shelters mainland wetlands and
estuarine environments from Gulf waves (USGS, 2017b).
Relative sea-level rise represents another ongoing environmental trend. As of 2023, NOAA’s
Dauphin Island tide-gauge product reports a historical mean sea-level rise trend of approximately
4.4 millimeters per year. This measurement reflects sea-level change relative to the land at the
                             Dauphin Island Gathering Partners

gauge and does not establish a land-subsistence rate throughout the Project area (NOAA, 2026c;
National Park Service, 2024). NOAA-supported modeling of Dauphin Island indicates that higher
sea levels can increase the locations affected by storm-driven dune overtopping and erosion that
extend the duration of these processes. Rising water levels consequently interact with episodic
storms to influence coastal flooding, shoreline stability, and overwashing of coastal dunes (NOAA,
2018).
Habitat restoration has also changed portions of the local environment. At Marsh Island in
Portersville Bay, a 2012 restoration fact sheet described historical shoreline losses of
approximately 5 to 10 feet per year. The restoration design included sediment placement, native
marsh planting, and a permeable segmented breakwater to establish additional marsh and protect
existing habitat. The fact sheet also documented oiling of Mississippi Sound marshes during the
Deepwater Horizon spill, while noting that oil did not come ashore on Marsh Island itself
(Deepwater Horizon Natural Resource Damage Assessment Trustees [Trustees], 2012). The
restoration project’s 2017 annual report records completion of 50 acres of restored tidal wetland
(Trustees, 2017). While not overlapping with the Project area, this provides a local example of
habitat restoration undertaken in response to regional resource injury and chronic erosion,
alongside the broader history of Alabama costal habitat loss.
Offshore sediment resources are another important component of establishing an environmental
baseline. The Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) identifies significant outer continent
shelf sediment deposits that can support coastal restorage, beach nourishment, and levee
reconstruction. Access to suitable material is constrained in some locations by existing oil and
gas infrastructure and other sensitive seabed uses. Protecting sediment availability therefore
connects offshore resource management with efforts to address coastal erosion, land loss,
flooding, and storm damage (BOEM, 2026). Approximately 17.75 miles of Line 11355 are located
within the Mobile Bay Significant Sediment Resource Area and would be removed as required by
BOEM.
The principal environmental concerns in the geographic vicinity of the Project area include
coastal flooding and storm-wave exposure, shoreline erosion, relative sea-level rise, loss or
alteration of wetland and barrier-island habitats, and competing uses of offshore sediment
resources. Their importance varies across the Project’s onshore, estuarine, and offshore settings.
Historical habitat conversion and erosion, subsequent restoration, and continuing shoreline and
water-level changes together characterize an environment shaped by both long-term processes
and discrete disturbances.

6. DIGP indicated that the Project would cross three impaired waterbodies including Porterville
Bay, the Mississippi Sound, and the Gulf of America. Given that the Project would involve piping
removal and jetting in the Mississippi Sound and Gulf of America, describe the potential effects
Project activities could have on these impaired waterbodies.
Response:
For the offshore portions of the Project that will be removed, there is potential for effects to
impaired waterbodies. During the jetting and removal of the piping, there will be seabed
disturbance. This disturbance can suspend sediment within the water column; however, this
impact would be localized to the project workspace and would be temporary as the suspended
sediments would resettle naturally. Additionally, there is the potential for a release of
hydrocarbons and hazardous lining material when jetting and removing piping. As discussed in
Section 1.3.2 of the originally filed Resource Report 1 (FERC Accession No. 20260731-5286),
DIGP would avoid this by wrapping the ends of the removed pipe segments with plastic and
securing them with duct tape. The remaining portions of open pipe that will be abandoned in place
will be plugged at subsea tie-ins and valves. To protect surface water resources in construction
and support areas from inadvertent releases of fuel and other mechanical fluids, DIGP has
prepared a Construction Spill Prevention and Response Procedures for Oil and Hazardous
Materials (Construction SPAR Plan) and submitted it with the July 31, 2026 Application in
Appendix 1B (FERC Accession No. 20260731-5286). The Construction SPAR Plan details
prevention, notification, and containment procedures to be followed by all personnel on the
Project.

7. For any offshore jetting required for abandonment activities:
       a. identify the days/weeks/months of anticipated jetting activities and anticipated
       construction hours associated with the activity (including the trench backfilling method);
       b. provide a list of each type of equipment and vessels anticipated to be used and the
       numbers of each type that would be deployed during construction; and
       c. describe the techniques that DIGP would use to minimize turbidity, noise, wildlife
       entanglement, and spills.
Response:
   a. Offshore jetting activities, including the trench backfilling method, are to occur during a
      24-hour daily period over 7 days a week, subject to weather conditions and other limiting
      factors in the Gulf. For distinct phases of construction over a weekly/monthly schedule,
      including offshore jetting activities, see the response to Comment No. 14.
   b. A list of each type of equipment and vessels to be used for the Project, including quantities
      and utilization by year, is provided in response to Comment No. 15.
   c. Descriptions of techniques to be utilized by DIGP for offshore jetting activities to minimize
      turbidity, noise, wildlife entanglement, and spills are provided below.
          i.     Turbidity
                 Offshore jetting associated with abandonment activities will utilize hand jetting
                 techniques designed to minimize turbidity. DIGP will first attempt removal of
                 offshore pipelines via pulling in areas with low cover to minimize seafloor
                 disturbance, and jetting will only be used where necessary. Jetting activities will
                 be limited to the minimum area and duration required to remove the pipeline,
                 thereby reducing sediment suspension and seafloor disturbance. Due to the minor,
                 short-term nature of the proposed disturbance and the naturally turbid waters
                 typical of the region, any increases in turbidity associated with the Project are
                 expected to be localized and temporary.
         ii.     Noise
                 The equipment that will be used will not generate significant underwater sound
                 pressure levels such as those typically associated with larger construction projects
                 including pile driving or large-scale dredging. Noise impacts will be minimized by
                 limiting the duration of jetting activities to the amount necessary to complete the
                 work. DIGP will first attempt removal via pulling rather than jetting. Support
                 vessels and jetting equipment will be operated only when needed to complete
                 abandonment activities. See Response 13 for noise impacts on wildlife.

iii.     Entanglement
         DIGP will minimize the potential for wildlife entanglement by following the NOAA
         Fisheries Protected Species Construction Conditions (Attachment 7.1). All in-
         water lines (including rope, chain, cable, and hose assemblies) will be maintained
         in a taut, non-looping configuration. Any flexible lines with the potential to loop
         or tangle will be enclosed within a sleeve or otherwise modified to increase rigidity
         and reduce entanglement risk. No unnecessary slack line will be permitted in the
         water, and all in-water equipment will be secured and monitored to minimize the
         potential for protected species entanglement or entrapment. In addition, turbidity
         curtains or other sediment barriers are not proposed for the Project, thereby
         eliminating the potential for protected species entanglement or entrapment
         associated with these barriers.
iv.      Spills
         To minimize impacts on fishery resources and aquatic habitat in the Project area,
         construction activities for the Project will adhere to the guidelines outlined in the
         Construction SPAR Plan, which includes measures for spill prevention,
         containment, and response. See Appendix 1B of the July 31, 2026 Application for
         DIGP’s Construction SPAR Plan (FERC Accession No. 20260731-5286). Spill
         prevention measures include routine inspection of tanks, containers, pumps, and
         transfer equipment; use of secondary containment; replacement of leaking or
         deteriorated containers; and implementation of fueling procedures. Spill response
         equipment will be maintained aboard support vessels, and fuel transfer hoses will
         be inspected and maintained in good working condition. In the event of a spill,
         response procedures will be followed in accordance with the Construction SPAR
         Plan to contain the release. The Williams Companies, Inc. Gulf of America
         Regional Oil Spill Response Plan (Attachment 7.2) provides an additional offshore
         spill contingency framework, including Incident Management Team
         responsibilities, agency notifications procedures, protection of environmentally
         sensitive areas, wildlife response measures, and deployment of response
         equipment. Vessel crew will be trained in spill prevention and response procedures
         and will follow all applicable regulatory requirements.

minimizing effects of light pollution on aquatic resources.

Vessel lighting associated with offshore construction activities will consist of U.S. Coast Guard-
required navigation and safety lighting, as well as topside deck and task lighting necessary for

To minimize impacts on threatened and endangered species potentially occurring within the action area,

Boat traffic is common in the vicinity of the Project; DIGP will ensure that all Project personnel are trained
in the identification of threatened and endangered species potentially occurring in the action area. DIGP’s
Wildlife and Vessel Strike Avoidance Plan and NOAA Fisheries SERO Vessel Strike Avoidance Measures
will be followed to minimize potential impacts to protected species. In accordance with DIGP’s Wildlife
and Vessel Strike Avoidance Measures, vessel operators and crews will maintain vigilant watch for the

 presence of marine mammals and giant manta rays. When possible, a Protected Species Observer/Marine
Mammal Observer will observe for protected species and reduce speed at night or during reduced visibility.
If a highly mobile protected species is sighted, a distance of 50 yards (150 feet) or greater must be
maintained between the animal and the vessel whenever possible. If a protected species is sighted while a
vessel is underway, vessels will attempt to remain parallel to the animal’s course and avoid excessive speed
or abrupt changes in direction. If any whales are sighted, a distance of 100 yards (300 feet) or greater will
be maintained. If a whale surfaces or approaches a vessel or is sighted within a vessel’s path, speed will be
reduced and the engine will be shifted to neutral if it is safe to do so, and engines will not be engaged until
the animals are clear of the area. Additionally, if whale mother/calf pairs, groups, or groups of dolphins are
observed near an underway vessel, speed will be reduced to 10 knots or less, while attempting to route
around the animals and maintaining a minimum distance of 100 yards whenever possible.

The gulf sturgeon is an anadromous subspecies of Atlantic sturgeon that occurs in coastal rivers, estuaries,
and nearshore marine waters of the Gulf of America from Lake Pontchartrain, Louisiana, to the Suwannee
River, Florida. Gulf sturgeon exhibit a predictable seasonal movement pattern: adults and subadults inhabit
freshwater rivers from approximately April through October, where they fast and rest in deep river pools,
and then migrate to estuarine and marine foraging habitats from approximately November through March,
where they actively feed on benthic invertebrates to regain body weight lost during their freshwater
residence period (USFWS and NMFS, 1995; NMFS and USFWS, 2022). Based on this seasonal pattern,
gulf sturgeons are most likely to be present in the offshore marine portion of the Project area during the
winter foraging period (approximately November through March). Although no designated critical habitat
occurs within the Project footprint, the Project area falls within the general range of gulf sturgeons that
utilize the northern Gulf of America coastal waters. Studies have documented gulf sturgeon use of Mobile
Bay and adjacent nearshore Alabama waters outside of designated critical habitat (Greenheck et al., 2023);
therefore, the potential for individual gulf sturgeon to occur in the Project area during the winter foraging
period cannot be dismissed. However, Project activities will primarily consist of pipeline abandonment in
the water column and on the seafloor, and will result in only temporary, localized disturbance to benthic
substrates. Gulf sturgeons are highly mobile and are not expected to experience significant disruption to
foraging behavior given the small and temporary nature of the disturbed area relative to the extent of
available foraging habitat in the northern Gulf of America. All Project impacts will be short-term, and the
benthic substrate is expected to recover to pre-construction conditions following completion of Project
activities. Based on the above analysis, the Project may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect, the gulf
sturgeon.
We believe the effect to ESA-listed species from the potential loss of nearshore habitat that could be used
for foraging or resting as a result of the proposed action is insignificant. No permanent habitat alteration
due to removal of the pipeline is anticipated. Individually and cumulatively when viewed on the areal scale,
we believe the Project will not appreciably reduce the abundance of estuarine and marine prey. Similar
habitat is located within and adjacent to the action area that protected species can use for foraging or refuge.
Overall, impacts on sea turtles and giant manta rays are anticipated to be insignificant as a result of the
Project’s activities; nevertheless, DIGP will implement measures designed to minimize potential impacts
to the greatest extent practicable. Per the NMFS Section 7 Consultation Guidance (2026c), if habitat is
present, it is predicted that individuals would avoid the area due to construction activities, then a may affect,
                                                       11
 not likely to adversely affect determination is appropriate. Based on this guidance as well as the mobility
of the species with potential to occur in the Project area and the likelihood that they will temporarily avoid
the area during Project activities, we have determined that the Project may affect but is not likely to adversely
affect the sea turtles, giant manta ray, Rice’s whale, sperm whale, oceanic white tip shark, and gulf sturgeon.
Gulf sturgeon critical habitat (68 FR 13370; March 19, 2003) is designated in 14 riverine, estuarine, and
marine units across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida; however, no designated gulf sturgeon
critical habitat units occur within the Project footprint. The nearest designated critical habitat is associated
with river systems east of the Project area (Pascagoula, Perdido, and Escambia River systems). The Project
area, including the nearshore Alabama state waters and offshore federal waters traversed by the Project, falls
outside of any designated critical habitat unit; therefore, the Project will have no effect on gulf sturgeon
critical habitat.
b. Routes of Effect to Critical Habitat
The project is located within boundary of proposed critical habitat for Rice’s whale (Gulf of America Unit).
The following physical or biological feature essential to the conservation of this species (“essential feature”)
is present in the Gulf of America Unit.
    Gulf continental shelf and slope associated waters between the 100 and 400 m isobaths that support
    individual growth, reproduction, and development, social behavior, and overall population growth.
The following attributes of this feature support Rice’s whales’ ability to forage, develop, communicate,
reproduce, rear calves, and migrate throughout the Gulf continental shelf and slope waters and influence
the value of the feature to the conservation of the species:
    1. sufficient density, quality, abundance, and accessibility of small demersal and vertically migrating
    prey species, including scombriformes, stomiiformes, myctophiformes, and myopsida;
    2. marine water with elevated productivity, bottom temperatures of 10–19ºC, and levels of pollutants
    that do not preclude or inhibit any demographic function; and
    3. sufficiently quiet conditions for normal use and occupancy, including intraspecific communication,
    navigation, and detection of prey, predators, and other threats.
Gulf continental shelf and slope associated waters between the 100-meter to 400-meter isobaths does occur
within the action area, however; as the maximum water depth within the Project area is approximately 200
feet (61 meters); therefore, the Project may affect but is not likely to adversely affect on Rice’s whale critical
habitat.
The project is located within boundary of proposed critical habitat for the green sea turtle, north Atlantic
distinct population segment (Unit NA01, Sargassum) is crossed by the Project. The Sargassum habitat is
defined as a developmental and foraging habitat for young green sea turtles, where surface waters form
accumulations of floating material, especially Sargassum. The following primary constituent elements
(PCEs) are present in Unit NA01:

    (i)      Convergence zones, surface-water downwelling areas, the margins of major boundary currents
             (Gulf Stream), and other locations where there are concentrated components of the Sargassum
             community in water temperatures suitable for the optimal growth of Sargassum and inhabitance
             of green sea turtles;
    (ii)     Sargassum in concentrations that support adequate prey abundance and cover;
    (iii)    Available prey and other material associated with Sargassum habitat, including, but not limited
             to, plants and cyanobacteria and animals native to the Sargassum community, such as hydroids
             and copepods; and
    (iv)     Sufficient water depth and proximity to available currents to ensure offshore transport (out of

                                                       12
              the surf zone) and foraging and cover requirements by Sargassum for post-hatchling green sea
             turtles (i.e., > 10-meter depth).

The Project would only potentially affect green sea turtle proposed critical habitat (Unit NA01) through
impacts to PCEs (ii) and (iii). Impacts to Sargassum habitat due to abandonment activities would only
occur through vessel traffic, as all other activities would occur on the ocean floor. Vessels that may
potentially drive through Sargassum mats are not anticipated to scatter the mats or harm organisms in the
Sargassum to the point of affecting the functionality of the green sea turtle proposed critical habitat PCEs.
Impacts from wakes and surface water disruption associated with these vessels would be temporary and
minor. Therefore, any potential disturbance would be temporary, minor, and insignificant, as it would not be
expected to result in adverse effects to the distribution, size, or composition of mats or their ability to support
green sea turtles or their prey resources.

Dear Mr. Klemm:

Dauphin Island Gathering Partners proposes to carry out the DIGP Abandonment Project (Project) as
described below. The Project is under the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
(FERC) and is being conducted pursuant to Section 7(b) of the Natural Gas Act.
DIGP acknowledges that designation of a non-federal representative by a federal agency must be in writing,
per 50 CFR 402.08 (Interagency Cooperation – Endangered Species Act (ESA) of 1973, as amended,
Designation of a Non-Federal Representative). However, per 18 CFR 380.13(b), Regulations
Implementing the National Environmental Policy Act, Compliance with the Endangered Species Act, the
Project sponsor (i.e., DIGP) is designated as FERC’s non-federal representative for the purpose of informal
consultations with the NMFS under the ESA. Therefore, by virtue of 18 CFR 380.13(b), FERC has
designated DIGP a non-federal representative for the purpose of conducting informal consultations under
Section 7 of the ESA and no further written documentation is necessary.
We request initiation of informal consultation under section 7(a)(2) of the ESA for the Project. We have
determined that the proposed activity may affect but is not likely to adversely affect the ESA-listed species
and critical habitat included in the table(s) below. Our supporting analysis is also provided below. We
request your written concurrence with these determinations.
Pursuant to our request for expedited informal consultation, we are providing, enclosing, or otherwise
identifying the following information:
            •   A description of the action to be considered;
            •   A description of the action area;
            •   A description of any listed species or critical habitat that may be affected by the action,
                and
            •   An analysis of the potential routes of effect on any listed species or critical habitat.
 Proposed Action
DIGP Dauphin Island Gathering Partners (DIGP) is filing with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
(FERC or Commission) an application pursuant to Section 7(b) of the Natural Gas Act and Section 157.18
of the Commission’s regulations seeking the issuance of an order authorizing the abandonment of
approximately 119.33 miles of existing natural gas pipelines and related appurtenances located in Mobile
County, Alabama, Alabama state waters, and Mobile and Main Pass Blocks of federal offshore waters.
Specifically, DIGP is requesting approval to:
        (i)    abandon in place and by removal approximately 3.88 and 0.04 miles, respectively, of
        onshore 20-inch-diameter pipeline on its existing DI001 (hereafter referred toas “Line 70”) in
        Mobile County, Alabama;
        (ii)   abandon in place and by removal approximately 3.43 and 0.05 miles, respectively, of
        onshore 24-inch-diameter pipeline on its existing DI002 (hereafter referred toas “Line 71”) in
        Mobile County, Alabama;
        (iii)   conduct activities associated with pipeline abandonment at the existing affiliate owned
        Coden Valve Yard and the existing DIGP Mobile Bay Gas Processing Plant where the existing
        Line 70 and Line 71 terminate, respectively, in Mobile County, Alabama;
        (iv)    abandon in place approximately 8.65 and 8.62 miles of the existing Line 70 and Line 71,
        respectively, in Alabama state waters, or 17.27 miles of total pipeline abandonment;
        (v)     abandon in place approximately 47.25 miles of offshore 24-inch-diameter pipeline on the
        existing PSN 11355 (hereafter referred to as “Line 11355”) in Alabama state waters and federal
        offshore waters, including disconnecting from the base of the riser at the MP-225 Platform;
        (vi)    abandon by removal approximately 17.75 miles of the existing Line 11355 within the
        Significant Sediment Resource Area (SSRA) in federal offshore waters;
        (vii)   abandon in place approximately 29.66 miles of offshore 20-inch-diameter pipeline on the
        existing PSN 10824 (hereafter referred toas “Line 10824”), including a disconnection from the
        subsea spool tie-in location at the MP-164 subsea valve tie-in and a disconnection from the riser
        base subsea spool at the MP-225 Platform in federal offshore waters; and
        (viii) abandonment of risers by removal at the AST-73 Platform, including abandonment by
        removal approximately 0.04 mile of piping associated with the tie-in to the riser and subsea spool
        sections of the AST-73 Platform in Alabama state waters.
The locations of the Project components are depicted in the attached mapping exhibits (Appendix 1).
Project activities are anticipated to occur between 2027 and 2031. DIGP anticipates construction may span
four years due to the logistics of offshore work and the safety considerations that could delay construction
depending on winter weather conditions in the Gulf of America.

Construction Procedures
Construction crews will mobilize offshore to federal waters via marine vessels to initiate abandonment
activities DIGP will complete depressurization, then pump the contents of the pipeline to downstream
piping and, if needed, a water outlet which will be filtered and dispose of in the Gulf of America when
below regulatory thresholds.
At the Line 70 and Line 71 connections at the AST-73 Platform, the Line 11355 connection at the MP-225
Platform, and the Line 10824 connection at the MP-225 Platform, the following activities are anticipated:
            •   Follow the riser down and jet out the tube turn.
               •    Cut out the tube turn including approximately 25 feet of pipe.
              •    Install a plumbers plug in the end of the pipe.
              •    Jet the end of the pipeline and install a layer of 3:1 sand-cement bags or sandbags over the
                   pipeline ensuring 3 feet of cover.
              •    Remove the tube turn and return to the support vessel.
DIGP will abandon the remaining pipelines in place prior to removal by cutting and plugging all
connections at subsea tie-ins and valves. Once all disconnections have been made, DIGP will begin pipeline
removal activities.
DIGP will remove approximately 17.75 miles of offshore pipelines, which includes the 0.04-mile piping
associated with the tie-in to the riser and subsea spool sections of the AST-73 Platform. Pipeline removal
will begin with mobilization of the pipeline removal barge spread, then anchors will be placed with the
assistance of an anchor handling tugboat. Divers are anticipated to hand jet the pipeline in order to provide
the location for placement of the jet sled, which will uncover the remaining pipeline segments. A
submersible pump may be utilized in localized areas where the depth of cover is greater than anticipated
and hand jetting is not feasible. A submersible pump disrupts the water bottom creating a dense slurry,
which is then suctioned and continuously pumped out into the water column. The pipeline will then be
retrieved utilizing a cut and remove or reverse lay method in between all crossings and SSTIs. After the
pipe has been retrieved, two joints in approximate 80-foot sections will be cut and placed in the pipe haul
barge. Retrieved pipe will be transferred from the retrieval barge to a secondary materials barge as needed.
DIGP proposes to remove the portion of the AST-73 Platform risers above water associated with Line 70
and Line 71. The lift boat will be mobilized to the AST-73 Platform. The 20-inch and 12-inch risers will
be cleaned and fully isolated before being cut above the surface of the water and removed.

Conservation Measures and Best Practices
To minimize impacts on threatened and endangered species potentially occurring within the Project area,
DIGP will ensure that all vessel operators implement the Wildlife and Vessel Strike Avoidance Plan, which
was developed based on recommendations from the USFWS as well as published NMFS guidance. The
avoidance and minimization measures outlined in this plan are further discussed below.
The West Indian manatee is the only listed marine mammal that commonly occurs within the Project area.
Suitable habitat for the West Indian manatee may be present within waters in the southern portion of the
Project area, such as Portersville Bay. On XXXX, DIGP submitted an informal coordination email to
USFWS Alabama Ecological Field Office to comply with requirements of Section 7 of the ESA. The letter
included a Project description, Project location map, DIGP’s assessment of impacts, and request for
concurrence with DIGP’s findings of not likely to adversely affect for the federally listed species identified
for the Project under USFWS jurisdiction, including the West Indian manatee. The gulf sturgeon is also
under the joint jurisdiction of USFWS and NMFS; NMFS is responsible for ESA Section 7 consultations
regarding gulf sturgeon and its critical habitat in marine units, and the Services divide responsibility in
estuarine units. DIGP is coordinating with USFWS separately regarding gulf sturgeon in estuarine and
riverine units through the USFWS Alabama Ecological Field Office.
Increases in turbidity associated with Project activities could temporarily cause protected species, including
dolphins, to relocate to nearby suitable habitat or avoid the Project area. Turbidity generated by Project
activities may extend beyond the immediate workspace; however, it is anticipated to quickly settle or
dissipate to ambient levels. Alabama coastal waters are naturally turbid, with high winds, storm events, and
tides causing clay-rich sediments to remain easily suspended, resulting in the characteristically muddy
waters of the region. Due to the highly localized and short-duration nature of Project activities, impacts on
dolphins and other protected species resulting from turbidity are anticipated to be negligible.
Impacts associated with construction noise will also be negligible, as protected species are expected to leave
the area when Project activities commence. The equipment to be used will not generate significant
underwater sound pressure levels comparable to those typically associated with larger-scale construction
projects, such as pile driving or large-scale dredging.
Boat traffic is common in the vicinity of the Project; DIGP will ensure that all Project personnel are trained
in the identification of threatened and endangered species potentially occurring in the Project area, and in
the Wildlife and Vessel Strike Avoidance Plan, to minimize potential impacts. Vessel operators and crews
will maintain vigilant watch for protected species. In accordance with DIGP’s Wildlife and Vessel Strike
Avoidance Measures, vessel operators and crews will maintain vigilant watch for the presence of marine
mammals and giant manta rays. If a dolphin or giant manta ray is sighted, a distance of 50 feet or greater
must be maintained between the animal and the vessel whenever possible. If a dolphin is sighted while a
vessel is underway, vessels will attempt to remain parallel to the animal’s course and avoid excessive speed
or abrupt changes in direction. If any whales are sighted, a distance of 100 yards or greater will be
maintained. If a whale surfaces or approaches a vessel or is sighted within a vessel’s path, speed will be
reduced and the engine will be shifted to neutral if it is safe to do so, and engines will not be engaged until
 the animals are clear of the area. Additionally, if whale mother/calf pairs, groups, or groups of dolphins are
observed near an underway vessel, speed will be reduced to 10 knots or less, while attempting to route
around the animals and maintaining a minimum distance of 100 yards whenever possible.
DIGP anticipates utilizing anchor vessels during offshore abandonment activities, which will impact the
seafloor (benthic habitat) where anchors are set and through cable sweeps as vessels reposition. The
locations where anchors are set cannot be predetermined, as anchor placement depends on weather,
currents, water depth, and proximity to existing third-party pipelines or other infrastructure; the quantity of
anchor drops will also depend on the abandonment activities being performed and the number of times a
vessel must be relocated. All impacts associated with anchor placement and lift boat stabilization (which
will disturb three areas of approximately 32 feet by 16 feet per lift boat) will be temporary, with the seafloor
expected to return to pre-construction conditions through normal tidal and wave action following
completion of Project activities.
Where feasible, DIGP will remove pipeline segments via pulling rather than jetting to minimize seafloor
disturbance and turbidity; jetting will be used only where pulling is not practicable, such as to expose cut
locations. A submersible pump may be utilized in localized areas where the depth of cover is greater than
anticipated and hand jetting is not feasible; impacts associated with submersible pump use are comparable
to jetting and are anticipated to be minor and temporary.
Consultation with NMFS under the Marine Mammal Protection Act (MMPA) is required if the Project
anticipates the unintentional "take" of marine mammals within a specified geographic region. Based on the
avoidance behavior, mobility, and avoidance measures discussed above, Project activities are not
anticipated to result in the "take" of marine mammals (50 CFR 216.3); therefore, no take permit or MMPA
consultation with NMFS is required.

Description of the Action Area
The action area is all areas to be affected by the Federal action and not merely the immediate area involved
in the action (50 CFR 402.02). Effects of the action are all consequences to listed species or critical habitat
that are caused by the proposed action, including the consequences of other activities that are caused by the
proposed action. A consequence is caused by the proposed action if it would not occur but for the proposed
action and it is reasonably certain to occur. Effects of the action may occur later in time and may include
consequences occurring outside the immediate area involved in the action. The action area is distinct from
and can be larger than the project footprint because some elements of the project may affect listed species
or critical habitat some distance from the project footprint. The action area, therefore, extends out to a point
where no effects from the Project are expected to occur.
For this Project, the action area includes onshore areas of Mobile County, Alabama; Alabama state waters;
and Mobile and Main Pass Blocks This area is within the Gulf of America and adjacent Alabama coastal
waters, including Portersville Bay and the Mississippi Sound, and is approximately bounded by Latitude
30.398794, -88.171252 and Longitude 29.624603, -88.454115. The nearest estuary/ocean inlet is Bayou
Como. Onshore, the Project crosses two HUC-12 subwatersheds: the West Fowl River-Frontal Fowl River
Bay subwatershed (HUC 031700090103) and the Dauphin Island subwatershed (HUC 031700090202). The
onshore action area extends along approximately 3.92 miles of Line 70 (DI001) and 3.48 miles of Line 71
(DI002), terminating at the existing Coden Valve Yard and Mobile Bay Gas Processing Plant, respectively,
including a segment beneath Highway 188. The action area is depicted in figures included in the Threatened
and Endangered Species Report (Attachment 1).
The Project's onshore and nearshore waterbody crossings include Bayou Como (a perennial, warmwater
stream supporting red drum, spotted seatrout, and Atlantic croaker), as well as Portersville Bay and the
Mississippi Sound, both of which the offshore portion of the Project crosses immediately upon leaving the
coastline. Portersville Bay and the Mississippi Sound are listed as impaired under Section 303(d) of the
Clean Water Act for E. coli, and the Gulf of America segment crossed by Line 11355 is listed as impaired
 for mercury; all crossings of these waterbodies will be abandoned in place or conducted using minimally
invasive methods, and impacts are not expected to contribute to existing impairments.
The offshore action area extends through Alabama state waters and into federal waters of the Gulf of
America, encompassing the abandonment of Line 70, Line 71, Line 11355 (PSN 11355), and Line 10824
(PSN 10824), as well as riser abandonment at the AST-73 Platform and equipment removal at the MP-225
Platform. A portion of Line 11355 (approximately 17.75 miles) lies within a Bureau of Ocean Energy
Management (BOEM)-designated Significant Sediment Resource Area (SSRA) and will be abandoned by
removal as required by BOEM. Three discrete 200-by-300-foot temporary workspaces will be used to
disconnect pipelines at the AST-73 Platform, the MP-225 Platform, and the MP-164 subsea valve tie-in.
Project vessels, including lift boats and 4-point and 8-point anchor vessels, will be used throughout the
offshore action area; anchor cable sweeps associated with these vessels may extend beyond the defined
workspace boundaries, though the extent of this disturbance cannot be predetermined and is discussed
qualitatively.
The offshore portion of the action area is characterized by unvegetated nearshore soft bottom, nearshore
pelagic, nearshore sand/shell bottom, and nearshore hardbottom habitats. No submerged aquatic vegetation,
seagrass beds, or mangroves are present (note: free-floating Sargassum surface habitat associated with
green sea turtle critical habitat Unit NA01 may be present in the offshore portion of the action area, as
discussed in the Critical Habitat section below). Sediments in the offshore action area are primarily
characterized by clays, with some sand; clays are fine-grained and cohesive and tend to remain suspended
in the water column longer than coarser, non-cohesive sediments such as sand, which resettle more quickly.
The shallow coastal waters of Alabama are naturally turbid, influenced by wind, precipitation, coastal
erosion, riverine sediment input (including from the West Fowl River and Bayou Como), and human
activity such as oyster dredging and recreational/commercial boating.
The onshore action area falls within the Southern Coastal Plain Level III Ecoregion and the Gulf Coast
Flatwoods and Gulf Barrier Islands and Coastal Marshes Level IV Ecoregions. Onshore habitat types
crossed by the Project include palustrine emergent (PEM), palustrine scrub-shrub (PSS), and palustrine
forested (PFO) wetlands, developed land, and forested upland. The offshore action area occurs within
designated Essential Fish Habitat for several federally managed species, including cobia, king mackerel,
blacktip shark, red snapper, brown shrimp, and white shrimp, among others. No Habitat Areas of Particular
Concern, as defined by NMFS, occur within the action area.
Access to offshore Project locations will occur via established marine vessel routes with sufficient water
depth that wheel washing is not required; therefore, no land or seafloor disturbance is anticipated as a result
of offshore access. Onshore access will primarily utilize existing public and private roads and the Line
70/Line 71 pipeline rights-of-way, supplemented by temporary access roads totaling 5.15 acres.

Effects of the Action
Based on range and habitat, sea turtles have the potential to occur within the Project area. The offshore
action area provides limited foraging habitat; however, nesting habitat is present in the vicinity of the
Project, as Dauphin Island — located adjacent to the onshore Project area — supports documented annual
nesting by loggerhead sea turtles, and occasional nesting by Kemp's ridley and green sea turtles (Alabama
Coastal Foundation, Share the Beach Program; NMFS, 2022; USFWS, 2023). Sea turtle nesting season
along the Alabama coast runs from May 1 through October 31. Accordingly, nesting females and hatchlings
may be present in nearshore Project waters during the construction period. Transient adults and subadults
may also occur in the offshore action area. The Project area is characterized by open water pelagic
environments and unvegetated benthic substrates including sand/shell bottoms and soft mud, which may
provide temporary resting or transit habitat for transient sea turtles. All impacts associated with the Project
will be short-term and temporary. The primary impact associated with Project activities will be disturbance
of the water bottom and temporary increases in turbidity. Other potential impacts on sea turtles and giant
manta rays include construction noise, avoidance behavior, and vessel strikes. No seagrass beds, reefs, or
other structured foraging habitats that would support resident sea turtle populations are present within the
Project area. During the nesting season (May 1 – October 31), DIGP will ensure that all artificial lighting
associated with onshore and nearshore Project activities is directed away from the beach and water to
minimize the potential for hatchling disorientation in accordance with NMFS and USFWS sea turtle
lighting guidelines.
Sea turtles and giant manta rays are highly mobile and are anticipated to leave the area if present at the start
of Project activities or avoiding the area if Project activities are already underway. All impacts on habitat
will be short-term and localized, quickly returning to pre-existing conditions following the completion of
Project activities. Turbidity generated by the Project activities may extend beyond the immediate
workspace; however, it is anticipated to quickly settle or dissipate to ambient levels. The activities
associated with the Project will be highly localized and of short duration, therefore, impacts on sea turtles
and giant manta rays resulting from turbidity are anticipated to be negligible. The Protected Species
Construction Conditions, NOAA Fisheries Southeast Regional Office also indicates concerns regarding
potential entanglement and entrapment of protected species with sediment barriers. No turbidity curtains
or other sediment barriers in which protected species could potentially become entangled or entrapped are
proposed for use on the Project.
Impacts associated with noise will also be negligible as sea turtles and giant manta rays are expected to
leave the area when Project activities commence. Further, the equipment that will be used will not generate
significant underwater sound pressure levels such as those typically associated with larger construction
projects including pile driving or large-scale dredging.
Potential impacts to sea turtles and manta rays associated with avoidance behavior vary based on several
factors including the cause of the behavior. For instance, passive avoidance of the area would result in less
 stress than an individual that is already present and inadvertently startled into leaving the area. In addition,
if a project is large-scale or there is not suitable habitat in the immediate vicinity of the activity, individuals
may have to travel greater distances to locate suitable habitat or be forced to occupy less suitable habitat.
Due to the localized nature of Project activities, as well as the abundance of available suitable habitat in the
surrounding area, impacts on sea turtles and giant manta rays associated with avoidance of the Project area
are anticipated to be negligible.
DIGP will ensure that all Project personnel are trained in the identification of threatened and endangered
species potentially occurring in the Project area, as well as the measures outlined herein. In accordance
with the NMFS’s Vessel Strike Avoidance Measures (2021), vessel operators and crews will maintain
vigilant watch for sea turtles and giant manta rays. If any of these species are sighted, vessel operators will
attempt to maintain at least 50 yards from sea turtles and 50 feet from giant manta rays while in transit.
Additionally, to minimize impacts on threatened and endangered species potentially occurring within the
Project area, DIGP will ensure that all vessel operators implement the Wildlife and Vessel Strike Avoidance
Plan, which was developed based on recommendations from the USFWS as well as published NMFS
guidance (see Attachment 1).
Overall, impacts on sea turtles and giant manta rays are anticipated to be negligible as a result of the
Project’s activities; nevertheless, DIGP will implement measures designed to minimize potential impacts
to the greatest extent practicable. Per the NMFS Section 7 Consultation Guidance (2023), if habitat is
present, it is predicted that individuals would avoid the area due to construction activities, then a may affect,
not likely to adversely affect determination is appropriate. Based on this guidance as well as the mobility
of the species with potential to occur in the Project area and the likelihood that they will temporarily avoid
the area during Project activities, we have determined that the Project may affect but is not likely to
adversely affect the sea turtles, giant manta ray, Rice’s whale, sperm whale, oceanic white tip shark, and
gulf sturgeon. Gulf sturgeon critical habitat (68 FR 13370; March 19, 2003) is designated in 14 riverine,
estuarine, and marine units across Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, and Florida; however, no designated
gulf sturgeon critical habitat units occur within the Project footprint. The nearest designated critical habitat
is associated with river systems east of the Project area (Pascagoula, Perdido, and Escambia River systems).
The Project area, including the nearshore Alabama state waters and offshore federal waters traversed by the
Project, falls outside of any designated critical habitat unit; therefore, the Project will have no effect on gulf
sturgeon critical habitat. Proposed critical habitat for Rice’s whale (Gulf of Mexico Unit, 100-meter to
400-meter isobath) does occur within the action area, however; as the maximum water depth within the
Project area is approximately 200 feet (61 meters); therefore, the Project will have no effect on Rice’s whale
critical habitat.
Federally designated critical habitat for the green sea turtle (Unit NA01, Gulf of America Sargassum) is
crossed by the Project. The Sargassum habitat is defined as a developmental and foraging habitat for young
green sea turtles, where surface waters form accumulations of floating material, especially Sargassum. The
following primary constituent elements (PCEs) are present in Unit NA01:

    (i)      Convergence zones, surface-water downwelling areas, the margins of major boundary currents
             (Gulf Stream), and other locations where there are concentrated components of the Sargassum
             community in water temperatures suitable for the optimal growth of Sargassum and inhabitance
             of green sea turtles;

    (ii)     Sargassum in concentrations that support adequate prey abundance and cover;

    (iii)    Available prey and other material associated with Sargassum habitat, including, but not limited
             to, plants and cyanobacteria and animals native to the Sargassum community, such as hydroids
             and copepods; and
     (iv)    Sufficient water depth and proximity to available currents to ensure offshore transport (out of
            the surf zone) and foraging and cover requirements by Sargassum for post-hatchling green sea
            turtles (i.e., > 10-meter depth).

The Project would only potentially affect green sea turtle proposed critical habitat (Unit NA01) through
impacts to PCEs (ii) and (iii). Impacts to Sargassum habitat due to abandonment activities would only
occur through vessel traffic, as all other activities would occur on the ocean floor. Vessels that may
potentially drive through Sargassum mats are not anticipated to scatter the mats or harm organisms in the
Sargassum to the point of affecting the functionality of the green sea turtle proposed critical habitat PCEs.
Impacts from wakes and surface water disruption associated with these vessels would be temporary and
minor. Therefore, any potential disturbance would be minor, as it would not be expected to result in adverse
effects to the distribution, size, or composition of mats or their ability to support green sea turtles or their
prey resources.

The gulf sturgeon is an anadromous subspecies of Atlantic sturgeon that occurs in coastal rivers, estuaries,
and nearshore marine waters of the Gulf of America from Lake Pontchartrain, Louisiana, to the Suwannee
River, Florida. Gulf sturgeon exhibit a predictable seasonal movement pattern: adults and subadults inhabit
freshwater rivers from approximately April through October, where they fast and rest in deep river pools,
and then migrate to estuarine and marine foraging habitats from approximately November through March,
where they actively feed on benthic invertebrates to regain body weight lost during their freshwater
residence period (USFWS and NMFS, 1995; NMFS and USFWS, 2022). Based on this seasonal pattern,
gulf sturgeons are most likely to be present in the offshore marine portion of the Project area during the
winter foraging period (approximately November through March). Although no designated critical habitat
occurs within the Project footprint, the Project area falls within the general range of gulf sturgeons that
utilize the northern Gulf of America coastal waters. Studies have documented gulf sturgeon use of Mobile
Bay and adjacent nearshore Alabama waters outside of designated critical habitat (Greenheck et al., 2023);
therefore, the potential for individual gulf sturgeon to occur in the Project area during the winter foraging
period cannot be dismissed. However, Project activities will primarily consist of pipeline abandonment in
the water column and on the seafloor, and will result in only temporary, localized disturbance to benthic
substrates. Gulf sturgeons are highly mobile and are not expected to experience significant disruption to
foraging behavior given the small and temporary nature of the disturbed area relative to the extent of
available foraging habitat in the northern Gulf of America. All Project impacts will be short-term, and the
benthic substrate is expected to recover to pre-construction conditions following completion of Project
activities. Based on the above analysis, the Project may affect, but is not likely to adversely affect, the gulf
sturgeon.
